To fix (2)

To fix Effect Sizes in t-tests and F-tests

What we found

We found 4 t-tests and/or F-tests where effect sizes are not reported. Check these tests in the table below, and consider adding effect sizes.

Show details

We recommend checking the sentences below, and add any missing effect sizes.
O teste t de Williams para correlações dependentes (Steiger, 1980) indicou que a correlação da SDO com a negação do preconceito foi significativamente maior do que a do RWA (0,67 vs. 0,46; t(96) = 2,80, p = 0,006), enquanto as correlações com ameaça (0,56 vs. 0,53; t(96) = 0,46, p = 0,647) e afirmação de diferenças (0,34 vs. 0,39; t(96) = -0,60, p = 0,551) não diferiram estatisticamente.
O teste t de Williams para correlações dependentes (Steiger, 1980) indicou que a correlação da SDO com a negação do preconceito foi significativamente maior do que a do RWA (0,67 vs. 0,46; t(96) = 2,80, p = 0,006), enquanto as correlações com ameaça (0,56 vs. 0,53; t(96) = 0,46, p = 0,647) e afirmação de diferenças (0,34 vs. 0,39; t(96) = -0,60, p = 0,551) não diferiram estatisticamente.
O teste t de Williams para correlações dependentes (Steiger, 1980) indicou que a correlação da SDO com a negação do preconceito foi significativamente maior do que a do RWA (0,67 vs. 0,46; t(96) = 2,80, p = 0,006), enquanto as correlações com ameaça (0,56 vs. 0,53; t(96) = 0,46, p = 0,647) e afirmação de diferenças (0,34 vs. 0,39; t(96) = -0,60, p = 0,551) não diferiram estatisticamente.
Em particular, os nordestinos foram classificados como um grupo menosprezado, apresentando uma carga fatorial de 0,62 na análise 1 Cabe observar que Souza et al. (2025) reportaram uma interação estatisticamente significativa entre a condição experimental e a dimensão de Incompetência, F(2, 228) = 3,48, p < 0,001.

For metascientific articles demonstrating that effect sizes are often not reported:

  • Peng, C.-Y. J., Chen, L.-T., Chiang, H.-M., & Chiang, Y.-C. (2013). The Impact of APA and AERA Guidelines on Effect Size Reporting. Educational Psychology Review, 25(2), 157–209. doi:[10.1007/s10648-013-9218-2](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-013-9218-2).

To fix Reproducibility Check

What we found

  • We assessed 6 R code files for reproducibility and ran them (each in an isolated Docker container).
  • 1 of 6 scripts ran without error when executed.
  • Of the others, 1 did not reproduce and 4 could not be checked automatically.
  • 10 installable dependencies detected.
  • 444 statistics stored from the extracted output; 0 of 7 reported tests matched (0%).

Note

See the section Reproducibility Check below for the details.

To check Codebook Check

What we found

  • We parsed 407 variable definitions from codebook/README files.
  • 406 of 514 data columns (79%) are documented in a codebook; 108 are not.
Show details

Q66_11 yes DWB11)Nós não vivemos em um mundo perigoso. Se as pessoas tomam algumas precauções, provavelmente nada de ruim acontecerá a elas. Q66_11 Study5Dataset.sav labelled

Absolute Paths

Best programming practice is to use relative file paths (e.g., ‘./files’) instead of absolute file paths (e.g., ‘C://Lakens/project_dir/files’) as these folder names do not exist on other computers. No absolute file paths were found in any of the code files.

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No setwd() calls were found in any of the code files.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). No install.packages() calls were found in any of the code files.

Libraries / Imports

Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In 1 code file, libraries/imports were at multiple places (i.e., with more than 3 non-comment lines in between).

This module assesses whether the paper’s code could be run on its data, and — because execute = TRUE — actually ran it. We examined 6 R code files.

Run order

The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), source() calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

Order File Runs after Basis
1 SyntaxStudy1.R — numeric
2 SyntaxStudy2.R — numeric
3 MultivariateMetaAnalysisStudy3.R — numeric
4 SyntaxStudy4.R — numeric
5 SyntaxStudy6.R — numeric
6 Nordestinos.R — none

File paths

The data paths in the code to files the repository holds work as deposited, but 1 path names a file the repository does not hold: bancoporpaiscomnomesparametaanalisemultivariada.csv. 8 data paths were built at runtime with sprintf()/paste()/file.path() instead of written as a literal path — this is fragile authoring practice (it silently breaks if the code is run from a different working directory than the author’s own). We resolved all of these on a best-effort basis.

Files the deposit does not hold

The scripts that did not run through read 1 data file that is not in the deposit, and no script of the deposit writes: bancoporpaiscomnomesparametaanalisemultivariada.csv.

Execution

The code was run. Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 6 scripts: 1 ran without error, 1 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. 4 scripts need a person to choose a file, answer a question or use an app, which cannot be reproduced without one: SyntaxStudy1.R, SyntaxStudy2.R, SyntaxStudy4.R, SyntaxStudy6.R. Naming the file in the script solves this.

File Outcome Detail Time (s)
SyntaxStudy1.R needs_a_person 0.6
SyntaxStudy2.R needs_a_person 0.6
MultivariateMetaAnalysisStudy3.R errored runtime 1.4
SyntaxStudy4.R needs_a_person 2.8
SyntaxStudy6.R needs_a_person 3.1
Nordestinos.R ran_ok 36.2

Calls that install packages in the code

2 calls to install.packages(), groundhog, checkpoint, renv, pacman and the like were replaced, since they install packages themselves: groundhog.library() and p_load() by library(), the others by a statement that does nothing. The scripts ran with the packages installed before the run.

> zs <- function(x) (x - mean(x)) / sd(x)
> fmt <- function(x, k = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = k)
> skew_g1 <- function(x) { m <- x - mean(x); mean(m^3) / mean(m^2)^1.5 }
> williams <- function(r12, r13, r23, n) {
>   detR <- 1 - r12^2 - r13^2 - r23^2 + 2 * r12 * r13 * r23
>   rbar <- (r12 + r13) / 2
>   t <- (r12 - r13) * sqrt((n - 1) * (1 + r23) /
>         (2 * (n - 1) / (n - 3) * detR + rbar^2 * (1 - r23)^3))
>   c(t = t, df = n - 3, p = 2 * pt(-abs(t), n - 3))
> }

> kurt_g2 <- function(x) { m <- x - mean(x); mean(m^4) / mean(m^2)^2 - 3 }
> nodot <- function(x, k = 2) sub("^(-?)0\\.", "\\1.", fmt(x, k))
> mns <- function(x) gsub("-", "\u2212", sub("^--$", "\u2014", x))
> star <- function(p) ifelse(p < .001, "***", ifelse(p < .01, "**", ifelse(p < .05, "*", "")))
> som_vars <- c(RWA = "Right-wing authoritarianism", SDO = "Social dominance orientation",

> cat("\nDangerous prejudice, Box-Cox robustness check:\n")

Dangerous prejudice, Box-Cox robustness check:
> for (s in studies) {
>   d <- dat[[s]]; y <- 8 - d$dangerous; n <- nrow(d)
>   ll <- function(l) { z <- if (abs(l) < 1e-8) log(y) else (y^l - 1) / l
>                       -n / 2 * log(mean((z - mean(z))^2)) + (l - 1) * sum(log(y)) }
>   lam <- optimize(ll, c(-5, 5), maximum = TRUE)$maximum
>   bc <- -(if (abs(lam) < 1e-8) log(y) else (y^lam - 1) / lam)
>   r_raw <- cor.test(d$ne, d$dangerous); r_bc <- cor.test(d$ne, bc); rho <- cor.test(d$ne, d$dangerous, method = "spearman", exact = FALSE)
>   w <- williams(cor(d$ne, d$derogated), cor(d$ne, bc), cor(d$derogated, bc), n)
>   cat(sprintf("Study %s: skew %s -> %s, kurtosis %s -> %s | r(ne) raw = %s (p = %.3f), Box-Cox = %s (p = %.3f), rho = %s (p = %.3f) | Williams derogated vs dangerous (Box-Cox) t(%d) = %s, p = %.2g\n",
>               s, fmt(skew_g1(d$dangerous)), fmt(skew_g1(bc)), fmt(kurt_g2(d$dangerous)), fmt(kurt_g2(bc)),
>               fmt(r_raw$estimate), r_raw$p.value, fmt(r_bc$estimate), r_bc$p.value, fmt(rho$estimate), rho$p.value,
>               n - 3, fmt(w["t"]), w["p"]))
> }

SPSS data

SPSS data and syntax (.sav + .sps) are present. This module does not execute SPSS syntax itself — the syntax is at least documented, but not run here. If an SPSS-Viewer file (.spv) is also deposited, its results are extracted directly (no execution needed); consider adding one if not. Consider depositing the analysis in jamovi (.omv) or JASP (.jasp) instead: these formats store the data and the analyses together in one file, so the results are reproducible from the file itself.

Mplus code, no reproducible output

2 Mplus code files are present, but this module has no way to extract statistics from Mplus output, and no self-reproducible output (JASP/jamovi, SPSS-Viewer, a Stata output log, or Mplus output) was found to fall back on. Consider depositing the analysis output (a rendered results/log file), or re-running the analysis in jamovi or JASP (free; the .omv/.jasp file bundles data and results together).

More detail

Ethics Approval Check

We did not detect an ethics approval statement, and this paper does not appear to involve live data collection from human or animal participants. Ethics approval is typically not required for theoretical work, simulations, reviews, meta-analyses, or secondary analyses of published data.

Power Analysis Check

No power analyses were detected.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.
